Rune’s Scroll

CTO Andrew Bosworth confirmed on Instagram that Horizon Worlds will stay on Quest VR headsets for existing games “for the foreseeable future,” walking back the shutdown announced just a day earlier after a strong community response. No new VR titles are planned, and Meta says most of its energy is going toward mobile.

Why it matters

If a guest asks whether Worlds is going away on Quest, the answer today is no — existing games keep working in VR, but don’t promise new VR-first titles.

Meta added new Skyler frame and lens combinations, including Shiny Chalky Gray with Transitions Sapphire lenses. Live translation — previously in early access — now rolls out to all markets across English, French, Italian, and Spanish.

Why it matters

Live translation across four languages is now a general feature, not an early-access demo — an easy one to show a guest live on the floor.

Meta’s wearables web-app toolkit added instructions letting Display web apps respond to Meta AI voice commands: the wearer speaks, Meta AI calls the app’s tools, and the app updates. It is off by default and enabled per device, and Meta stresses apps must stay fully usable by D-pad with no assistant at all.

Why it matters

Web apps on the Display glasses can gain voice control — but every app must still work completely by D-pad, which is how you’ll demo them.

Simply (Simply Piano, Simply Guitar) is building Display-glasses experiences that show chords, lyrics, and tuning guidance hands-free in the wearer’s field of view, with real-time audio recognition giving feedback as they play. It was showcased at Meta Connect 2026.

Why it matters

A concrete “what is a display for” example: hands-free guidance while your hands are busy — music practice is an easy story to tell.

From Connect: a photorealistic, voice-driven hologram for video calls (WhatsApp early access, US, this fall); cycling and transit directions by voice; an Explore app for finding Display experiences; Dolby Atmos capture; photo editing on the display; and expansion to the UK, Canada, France, Italy, and Germany.

Why it matters

These are the Display updates guests will ask about — hologram calls and hands-free navigation are the two to lead with.

The glasses have no display: cameras, microphones, and speakers work with Gemini while a connected Galaxy phone handles the heavier AI tasks. FCC filings show the hardware has passed certification. A Samsung official gave the November target to The Korea Herald, but Samsung has not formally announced a date.

Say it like this

“Samsung’s are capture-and-audio glasses — nothing in your view. Different job from the Display; which matters more to you?”

Apple is said to have shelved the lower-cost Vision successor and shifted focus to AI smart glasses, putting it in more direct competition with Meta, Google, and Samsung. This rests on industry sources via TheElec and is unconfirmed — treat it as a rumor until Apple says otherwise.

Say it like this

“That’s still a rumor, not an Apple announcement. What we can compare today is what’s actually shipping.”

Trend data shows Steam Frame as the one headset name with real search momentum this year, while generic headset interest cools. Buyers are searching for specific named products, not categories.

Say it like this

“People look up the product they’ve already heard about — name recognition is doing the heavy lifting in VR right now.”

Buyers are searching for named products instead of categories, and Meta’s glasses lead that mindshare at 1.5 million searches, up 82%.

Say it like this

“Most guests walk in already knowing the name — our job is fit, prescription, and battery questions, not awareness.”

Sony is exhibiting its Glasstron, HMZ series, and SmartEyeglass as part of the exhibition “XR and AI: The Next Computing Frontier,” tracing the arc of head-mounted displays from Ivan Sutherland’s 1968 rig to today’s AI glasses.

Say it like this

“Sixty years of head-mounted displays got us here — today’s glasses are the first ones people actually want to wear all day.”
